zh_summary: @aleabitoreddit 引述路透社報道：10 月 22 日，高盛追蹤的多空、系統化及多策略對沖基金自新冠崩盤以來首次全部單日虧損超過 1%；科技型基金 10 月下跌約 10%，亞洲型基金下跌約 9%。Citadel 與摩根大通表示，散戶一直在逢低買入半導體、新雲端及記憶體股，買得最多的是 $NBIS、$SNDK 和 $TSM。他認為大量拋售並不理性，主要由對沖基金去槓桿推動。
en_summary: @aleabitoreddit cites a Reuters piece: on Oct 22, long/short, systematic and multi-strategy hedge funds tracked by Goldman Sachs all lost more than 1% in one day for the first time since the COVID crash; tech-focused funds are down about 10% in October and Asia-focused about 9%. Citadel and JPMorgan say retail has been buying the dip in semis, neoclouds and memory, mostly $NBIS, $SNDK and $TSM. He thinks much of the selling is irrational and driven by hedge fund deleveraging.
text:
Pretty crazy Reuters piece on the global selloff.

- October 22 marked the 1st time since the COVID crash that long/short, systematic, and multi-strategy hedge funds tracked by Goldman Sachs ALL lost more than 1% in a single day.

- Tech-focused hedge funds: down ~10% in October

- Asia-focused hedge funds: down ~9% in October

There’s separate interviews where Citadel/JP Morgan have been saying retail has been the ones buying the dip in semiconductor, neocloud, and memory stocks.

And the stocks bought by most retail were $NBIS, $SNDK, and $TSM.

Reuters stated this downturn triggered institutional deleveraging events among hedge funds.

Quite the divergence, I do think there’s been a ton of irrational selling now, hedge fund deleveraging seems to be a major contributor.

The selloff was fueled by concerns over AI spending and profitability, with Meta $META dropping 7% despite beating revenue expectations, as investors questioned its massive AI investments and negative free cash flow. Semiconductors were hit hardest, with the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index falling 6.7%, led by AMD $AMD (-8%), Micron $MU (-6%), and NVIDIA $NVDA (-4%). AI and chip stocks accounted for roughly 90% of the Nasdaq 100's losses. However, broader market participation remained positive, with the Dow and Russell 2000 gaining. Meanwhile, Brent crude surged 4% toward $113 amid Middle East tensions. Despite the decline, the Nasdaq remains up 11.9% YTD, sitting 5.8% below its October 6 record high.

en_summary: @aleabitoreddit: $ESMT and his legacy memory names held up better than the AI trade, with ESMT around 1.6x run rate P/E; ESMT expects legacy memory tightness through 2028 or longer plus further Q4 price increases.
text:
Actually $ESMT and my legacy memory names held up better than the rest of the AI trade. 

Probably did better... since ESMT is around 1.6x runrate P/E, annualized off July earnings.

This was more of a durability/PSMC hike sensitivity type thesis, but... we got durability support now from brand new commentary yesterday:

- ESMT expected tightness on their legacy memory products through 2028 or longer
- Further Q4 price increases... with the operating performance is expected to be better than the third quarter
- Supply shortfall exceeding 30%

Source: Digitimes TW

So you have a $2.15B MC company that made $107M net income a month (annualized $1.28B earnings a year) from July earnings... 

With future price hikes and likely tightness lasting through 2028 onward.

name: Serenity
zh_summary: @aleabitoreddit：$NVDA黃仁勳對CNBC表示2029年前記憶體供過於求不太可能，因為記憶體永遠可用得更多，並以數據中心使用LPDDR為例，反駁韓國媒體2029年將陷入紅海的看法。
en_summary: @aleabitoreddit: $NVDA Jensen Huang told CNBC a memory oversupply by 2029 is unlikely because you can always use more memory, citing LPDDR use in data centers, rebutting a Korean view of a 2029 red ocean.
text:
$NVDA Jensen Huang: Surplus of memory supply is unlikely by 2029. 

The CNBC question referenced a Korean newspaper opinion on $KOSPI / Samsung / SK Hynix that predicted "new supply will leave the memory sector a red ocean in 2029."

"One of the things that's really great about memory is that you can always use more of it", Jensen said, citing LPDDR usage in DCs.  And responded "I don't think so" in terms of possibilities of oversupply in 2029. 

Just my personal opinion, Nvidia probably has the most visibility in the entire industry. 

Especially around supply procurement and emerging capacity, given they're the ones leading all the architectural shifts. 

On durability, you have Samsung already allocated majority of capacity into 2031 from SED and hyperscalers like $GOOGL are already reportedly securing memory LTAs into 2035 from KeyBanc. 

Yet there's endless "it's all over" sentiment on memory now. I'd probably trust Jensen's opinion here.
